meta.title: The Estus Sensory Profile
meta.promise: Understand your sensory world in about 7 minutes. Free, private, yours to keep.

is: A free self-discovery tool that maps how you take in and respond to the world through your senses.
A gentle conversation starter you can keep, share, or bring to an appointment.
Strengths-first. Every pattern it describes comes with things it gives you, not just things it costs you.
isNot: It is not a diagnosis, and it is not a test you can pass or fail.
It is not normed against other people, so it never says you are more or less than anyone else.
It is not a substitute for an occupational therapy assessment. It is a doorway toward one if you want it.

adult.label: For teens & adults
adult.blurb: Answer for yourself. A supporter can help if you like.

kids.label: For kids
kids.blurb: A parent or carer can answer, or you can do it together.

caregiver.label: I'm a parent or carer answering about a child
caregiver.blurb: You'll read short statements about your child and pick how often each one fits.

together.label: We're doing it together with the child
together.blurb: Simple words, bigger buttons, and only three choices. There are no wrong answers. You can stop anytime and come back.

sections.title: Sound & light

sections.title: Touch & taste
sections.micro: There are no right answers here. Just what feels true for you.

sections.title: Movement & your body
sections.micro: How your body likes to move, and how it reads the space around it.

sections.title: Inside signals
sections.micro: The quieter signals from inside your body and your feelings.

wordings.A: Everyday sounds — chewing, humming, appliances, repetitive noises — feel intrusive and hard to filter out.
wordings.C: My child gets upset or distracted by everyday sounds others tune out (chewing, fans, humming).
wordings.K: Little sounds, like people chewing or buzzing things, really bug me.

wordings.A: I use background sound (music, TV, white noise, a fan) to help me focus or feel settled.
wordings.C: My child seeks out sound — hums, makes noises, or wants music or TV on to stay settled.
wordings.K: I like having music or sounds on. It helps me feel good.

wordings.A: In group conversations or noisy rooms, I struggle to separate voices from background noise.
wordings.C: My child struggles to follow what people say when there's background noise.
wordings.K: When it's noisy, it's hard to hear what people are saying to me.

wordings.A: Bright lights, fluorescent lighting, or visually busy spaces drain me quickly.
wordings.C: My child squints, shields their eyes, or gets tired and irritable in bright or visually busy places.
wordings.K: Bright lights or really busy, colourful places make my eyes and head tired.

wordings.A: I don't notice visual details or changes around me unless someone points them out.
wordings.C: My child walks past things — new objects, messes, obstacles — without seeming to notice them.
wordings.K: I don't really notice when things around me change or move.

wordings.A: Clothing textures, tags, seams, or certain fabrics bother me enough that I choose clothes around them.
wordings.C: My child refuses certain clothes because of tags, seams, or how the fabric feels.
wordings.K: Some clothes feel scratchy or wrong, and I don't want to wear them.

wordings.A: I seek out deep pressure or touch — tight blankets, firm hugs, fidgeting with textures — to feel calm.
wordings.C: My child seeks out squeezes, tight hugs, heavy blankets, or things to fidget with.
wordings.K: Big squeezy hugs or cosy tight blankets help me feel calm.

wordings.A: Unexpected or light touch (someone brushing past, light tickles) is uncomfortable or startling.
wordings.C: My child pulls away or gets upset at unexpected or light touch, like someone brushing past.
wordings.K: When someone touches me and I'm not ready, I don't like it.

wordings.A: Strong smells — perfume, cleaning products, certain foods — affect my mood or make spaces hard to be in.
wordings.C: My child notices and reacts strongly to smells other people barely register.
wordings.K: Strong smells make me feel yuck or make me want to leave.

wordings.A: I stick to familiar "safe foods" and find some food textures or flavours hard to tolerate.
wordings.C: My child eats a small range of safe foods and finds new textures or flavours hard.
wordings.K: I like my usual foods. New or mushy or lumpy foods are hard for me.

wordings.A: I feel better when I'm moving — rocking, pacing, bouncing my leg, exercising.
wordings.C: My child is happiest in motion — spinning, jumping, climbing, rocking, running.
wordings.K: Moving my body — jumping, spinning, wiggling — feels really good.

wordings.A: I feel uneasy with heights, lifts, escalators, or fast unexpected movement.
wordings.C: My child is cautious or fearful on swings, slides, escalators, or when their feet leave the ground.
wordings.K: Swings, slides, or being up high can feel scary to my body.

wordings.A: I misjudge force or distance — bumping into doorframes, gripping too hard, dropping things.
wordings.C: My child bumps into things, plays too rough without meaning to, or misjudges how hard to push or hold.
wordings.K: I bump into things a lot, or squeeze things too hard by accident.

wordings.A: I chew on things, press hard when writing, or hold tension in my body without realising.
wordings.C: My child chews on clothing or objects, pushes hard on pencils, or crashes into furniture on purpose.
wordings.K: I like chewing on things or crashing into soft stuff.

wordings.A: I don't notice hunger, thirst, or needing the toilet until it's urgent.
wordings.C: My child doesn't seem to notice hunger, thirst, or needing the toilet until the last minute.
wordings.K: Sometimes I don't know I'm hungry or need the toilet until it's really big.

wordings.A: I find it hard to tell what emotion I'm feeling until it's already overwhelming.
wordings.C: My child goes from seeming fine to very upset quickly, as if the feeling arrived all at once.
wordings.K: Sometimes big feelings surprise me — I don't know they're coming until they're huge.

wordings.A: I notice my body's early stress signals — heart rate, breathing, muscle tension — before they escalate.
wordings.C: My child can tell someone, or show, when their body is starting to feel stressed or "too much."
wordings.K: I can tell when my body starts feeling wobbly or too-much, before it gets really big.

wordings.A: Feeling too hot, too cold, or physically uncomfortable strongly affects my ability to function.
wordings.C: Being too hot, too cold, or physically uncomfortable derails my child's whole day.
wordings.K: When I'm too hot or too cold or itchy, everything gets harder.

wordings.A: People say they've called my name or spoken to me and I didn't notice.
wordings.C: My child often doesn't respond when their name is called, especially when focused.
wordings.K: Sometimes people say they called me, but I didn't hear them.

wordings.A: I can focus deeply on things that interest me even in environments that distract other people.
wordings.C: When my child is absorbed in something they love, the rest of the world disappears.
wordings.K: When I'm doing my favourite thing, I don't notice anything else.

wordings.A: Certain places — supermarkets, shopping centres, open-plan offices — are hard mainly because of the sensory load.
wordings.C: Busy places like supermarkets or parties reliably lead to distress for my child.
wordings.K: Big busy places like the shops feel like too much for me.

wordings.A: I plan my day or route around avoiding specific sensory situations.
wordings.C: My child avoids or resists specific places or activities because of how they feel, sound, or smell.
wordings.K: There are places or things I say "no" to because they feel too much.

wordings.A: When I control a space, I adjust it to suit me — lighting, sound, seating, temperature.
wordings.C: My child sets up their own spaces carefully — den-building, lights off, door closed, particular arrangements.
wordings.K: I like making my space just right — like cosy corners or lights off.

wordings.A: I'm drawn to intense sensory experiences — spicy food, loud music, fast rides, cold water.
wordings.C: My child loves big sensations — rough play, loud music, strong flavours, fast rides.
wordings.K: I love big exciting feelings — going fast, loud songs, splashing!

wordings.A: Small unexpected changes to plans or environments take a surprising amount of energy to manage.
wordings.C: Small changes to routine or environment cost my child a lot — even "good" surprises.
wordings.K: When things change and I wasn't ready, it feels hard inside.

wordings.A: After busy or loud environments, I need quiet recovery time before I can do anything else.
wordings.C: After busy days — school, parties, outings — my child needs downtime and may fall apart at home.
wordings.K: After a big loud day, I need quiet time to feel like me again.

wordings.A: When overloaded, I tend to go quiet, withdraw, or shut down rather than getting visibly upset.
wordings.C: When it's all too much, my child goes quiet, hides, or shuts down rather than acting out.
wordings.K: When everything is too much, I go quiet or want to hide.

wordings.A: I hide or suppress my sensory reactions around other people — and pay for it later.
wordings.C: My child holds it together in public or at school, then releases it all in their safe place.
wordings.K: I keep my "too much" feelings inside at school, and they come out at home.

wordings.A: Sensory factors — noise, light, textures, temperature — make it hard to fall or stay asleep.
wordings.C: Sensory things — pyjama textures, sounds, light, temperature — make sleep hard for my child.
wordings.K: Sounds or itchy pyjamas or light make it hard for me to sleep.

wordings.A: Certain sensory experiences bring me deep joy or comfort — specific music, textures, water, nature.
wordings.C: Certain sensory experiences light my child up — specific songs, textures, water play, spinning things.
wordings.K: Some feelings are my favourite ever — like water, or my special song, or soft things.
